idiom_name: trait implementor injected into an abstract class
implementation_notes: The implementor is a trait with abstract members and the abstraction is an abstract class (or another trait) holding it as a constructor parameter; Scala's primary decomposition tool is the trait and classes sit at the leaves of the inheritance model, so refined abstractions usually come from mixin composition rather than a deep class chain. What replaces the classic structure is constructor-injected trait values plus mixin composition; the cake pattern - abstract val/def members with self-type annotations - is the alternative wiring mechanism when dependencies must be assembled from modules, and it is compile-time checked but initialisation-order sensitive. Keep plain constructor injection unless the wiring is genuinely modular: the cake pattern's failure mode is a val that is still null because it was constructed before its dependency.
code_sketch:
trait Renderer:                                   // Implementor (Scala 3)
  def circle(r: Double): Unit

abstract class Shape(val renderer: Renderer):     // Abstraction
  def draw(): Unit

final class Circle(renderer: Renderer, radius: Double) extends Shape(renderer):
  def draw(): Unit = renderer.circle(radius)
pitfalls: Self-type (cake) wiring is compile-time checked but initialisation-order sensitive: a required member declared as a val can be null when a dependent val initialises, so declare requirements as def and provided members as lazy val.

Trait linearisation decides which mixin runs: an abstract override modifier must be mixed in after the base implementation or it never executes, and calling self.f instead of super.f recurses until the stack overflows.
Structural types look like a duck-typed implementor but compile to reflective calls unless the compiler is told otherwise, so explicit traits are usually cheaper and safer.
